summary: AA1 is genuinely closed and the replacement is correct in this project's own vocabulary. docs/research/30-design-space/07-pluggable-store-abstraction.md:151-155 writes CountingBinStore(GoverningBinStore(...)) and calls it 'Counting outside governing', so OUTSIDE means the enclosing decorator; the new comment (FaultInjectingStore.java:36-56) maps ABOVE onto the enclosing position and BELOW onto the delegate position, and both descriptions of what each measures are true of this code: with the meter as the delegate it sees the ambiguous landing write and the duplicate retry (both call delegate.* before/after the throw) and does not see an `unreachable` that threw before delegating; with the meter enclosing, it sees exactly the caller's calls and none of the injector's additions. The M4.9 claim is accurate: backlog.md:262 says M4.9 is 'Asserted by REQUEST COUNT through CountingBinStore', which is a claim about what the sequencer's recovery issues, and the enclosing position is the one that counts caller-issued reads -- including attempts an injected `unreachable` prevents from reaching the store, which is what would otherwise let an unbounded retry loop look bounded. The staged test that does assert the injector's own added request (FaultInjectingStoreTest:200) uses the other order, consistent with the comment's guidance. AA2 closed: the row (backlog.md:265) names all five staged Java files -- the decorator (as 'The FAULT-INJECTING STORE: a BinStore decorator'), FaultInjectingStoreTest, FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest, FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest and FaultFixtures -- and says FIVE FILES; the arithmetic checks out against `git diff --cached --stat`. AA4 closed: CommitProtocolSimulation is genuinely untracked and M4.16 now discloses it in the same shape as M4.19 and M4.20, with no measurement quoted above the disclosure. The withheld-write gap now has an owner in M4.13's row, and the M4.16 row it needed also closes a dangling ID -- HEAD referenced M4.16 from M4.17's row with no M4.16 row in the file. AA3's javadoc claim is TRUE as to fact: `injected` is a plain ArrayList and `drawCounts` a plain TreeMap (FaultInjectingStore.java:110-111), nothing synchronises them, and the three streams are drawn in per-call order, so replay does require one driving thread; the advice to M4.20 (interleave pods logically, one call at a time, rather than one virtual thread per pod) is sound and cites M4.20's row correctly -- that row does say 'many logical pods ... driven through the Sequencer seam'. Its reassurance overstates, which is F1. RED RECORDS: verified rather than taken on report. `git diff` against the index is empty, so the staged bytes are the bytes on disk; the three test classes' mtimes are 1788520127 and FaultFixtures' is 1788520621, both older than the round-11 verdict artifact .harness/review/30c96eff...reviewer.json at 1788520979, while only FaultInjectingStore.java and backlog.md (both 1788521065) postdate it -- so no test file changed this round. Independently, every one of the 22 @Test methods across the three staged classes (13 + 5 + 4, matching the 22 the runner reports) has an entry in .harness/tdd/red.json naming that file as its source; 10 stale entries name tests that were renamed away, which demands nothing. MUTANTS: six applied to the edited decorator, each reverted with `git checkout --`, all six killed by a named test -- putIfMatch's three alignment draws moved below the ambiguous branch (everyClassDrawsOnEVERYFaultingCallSoNoClassCanBeSKIPPEDSilently), the ambiguous putIfAbsent landing degraded to delegate.put (anAmbiguousPutIfAbsentSTILLLOSESToAnOccupiedSlot), scramble replaced by seed*3+stream (theTHREEFaultStreamsAreINDEPENDENTCoinsAndNotOnePhaseLocked), injected() returning the live list (two tests), get() made a pass-through (two tests), and the duplicate second write deleted (aDUPLICATEDPutREALLYREACHESTheStoreTwiceAndTheFirstResultIsWhatTheCallerGets). COST: nothing here changes an object-store request rate. All five files are test-only; the decorator's extra requests scale with faulted conditional writes, not with records, shards, partitions or indices; the read verbs it faults (stat, get, list) are exactly the three the sequencer's recovery uses -- ChainReplay.java:99,257,267,328 and CommitLog.java:177 -- and getRange, which it does not fault, is used by neither, so the row's 'the three read verbs recover walks a chain with' is accurate. NOT re-raised, deliberately: the unused imports in the three test classes and FaultFixtures' javadoc calling `read` shared by all three when FaultInjectingStoreStreamsTest imports and never calls it were both observed and declined at round 11, and Z4's structural half is unchanged. Rule 11 says a minor lands. ROUNDS: this is round 12 against rule 12's cap of two, and the mechanism is visible in the artifact trail -- rounds 3-12 each found a defect in the previous round's prose (the file's own comments say so at :117, :171, :182 and :208), which is precisely what rule 11 predicts when minors are fixed rather than recorded. All three findings below are minor. The right move is to land this and record them in the commit body, not to open a round 13 whose surface would be the prose of their fix.

findings.title: The threading javadoc added for AA3 names the two unsynchronised structures and then reassures the reader that the only casualty is reproducibility, which is not true of the structures it just named.
findings.detail: The note says 'injected is a plain ArrayList, drawCounts a plain TreeMap' and closes with 'Concurrency there would not corrupt the store, it would corrupt REPRODUCIBILITY'. The second half is right about the delegate and wrong about the injector's own state: concurrent ArrayList.add can drop an element or throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from inside the store call, and concurrent TreeMap.merge can lose an increment or leave the tree structurally inconsistent. Those two structures are not bookkeeping -- the class javadoc (:29-34) says being able to ASSERT which fault a run saw is the only defence against a silent simulator, and injected()/drawCounts() are how that assertion is made. The round-2 review of this file (artifact 2f893cc26126, finding R7) had already named 'an ArrayList losing or corrupting entries under concurrent add'; the prose written to close that finding now under-states it.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.20's author reads this note, judges that losing replay is an acceptable price for a stress run, and gives each logical pod its own virtual thread. Two pods call putIfAbsent at once and one injected record is lost, so M4.20's anti-vacuity assertion ('this run really did inject something') fails on a run that did inject something -- or injected.add throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException out of putIfAbsent, which the sequencer under test sees as an unexpected RuntimeException from the store and the sweep reports as a protocol failure. Both are the 'defect the harness fabricated' that FaultInjectingStoreDelegationTest's own javadoc (:31-36) says costs whole rounds to diagnose.
findings.recommendation: One clause, not a fix to the code: say that a race also loses or corrupts the record itself and can throw out of a store call. Per review.md rule 11 this lands as a minor; if it is touched at all it should be the same edit that M4.20 makes when it writes the driver.

findings.title: CARRIED OVER, previously filed as R8 and never re-filed: the clean putIfAbsent path buffers the body and re-declares its length, so the decorator accepts a write a real store refuses -- re-measured here so it survives into the commit body.
findings.detail: putIfAbsent reads the body through the private read(Body) helper (:263-267) on EVERY call, including the no-fault path, and re-wraps it as `new Body(bytes.length, ...)`. read() uses body.open().get().readAllBytes(), bypassing Body.checkedStream(), which Body's javadoc (binstore-spi/.../Body.java:31-33) calls 'the sanctioned path for a streaming backend' precisely because it REFUSES a body whose length disagrees with what it declared. Re-declaring the length as the observed byte count discards the caller's declaration. Two consequences: the clean path is not the undecorated path (putIfMatch's clean path at :314 passes the caller's Body straight through, so the two verbs differ), and the whole body is materialised in heap on every conditional write -- the thing Body exists to make unrepresentable (constraint C8, Body.java:11-16). Body's contract already says 'The supplier may be called more than once', so neither the duplicate nor the ambiguous arm needs the buffer either. This was filed as R8 (minor) at artifact 2f893cc26126, observed still open at 213e8b1e9331, and correctly not re-filed under rule 11 -- but the commit has not landed, so it is restated here with a measurement so that it reaches the commit body rather than only a gitignored artifact.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED with a temporary probe (created, run, deleted; tree restored): a Body declaring 17 bytes over a 12-byte stream is refused by MemoryBinStore directly -- 'body declared 17 bytes but yielded 12' -- and ACCEPTED through FaultInjectingStore's clean path, stored at size 12. So a production declared-length bug, a class of bug this repository has already had once (MemoryBinStore.java:130-138 records M2.0's round-1 finding about exactly such a body), fails every other T1 test and PASSES M4.13's 1,000-seed sweep, because the harness repairs it on the way through. That is the 'simulation proves the simulator' failure this file's own javadoc is written against, arriving through the clean path rather than through a probability.
findings.recommendation: Not blocking and not for this round. Pass the caller's Body through on both clean paths, and where a buffer is genuinely needed read via body.checkedStream() and re-wrap with body.length() rather than bytes.length. Natural home is M4.13's row, which already owns the other harness-fidelity gap (the withheld write).

findings.title: M4.13's row absorbed four separable deliverables, three of which are decorator work, which is the shape rule 12 was written from and the shape M4.12 has just spent twelve rounds demonstrating.
findings.detail: As staged, M4.13 owns: the 1,000-seed sweep with its <60s budget, configurable seed count and pinned per-seed regressions; delayed writes; reordered completions; partitioned leaders as an injectable fault, which the row itself says 'needs the store to know WHICH pod is calling and needs putIfMatch to be able to fail cleanly'; and the withheld-write Mode.LOST arm. The last four all mean re-opening FaultInjectingStore.java and re-testing it -- the file this task took twelve rounds to land -- while the first is a measurement task with a time budget. Moving them out of a closed row was right; putting all of them on the sweep is what makes the next commit large.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 is picked up as one commit: it extends the fault model in three directions, teaches the store which pod is calling, adds a clean-failure arm to putIfMatch, and then has to show 'each fault class has at least one seed where it changes the outcome' plus a 1,000-seed run under 60 seconds. Round one finds a defect in the new fault classes, round two finds a defect in round one's fix, and the row hits rule 12's cap for the same reason M4.12 did -- the review cost is paid again instead of learned from.
findings.recommendation: A separate row for the fault-model extension (delayed writes, reordered completions, pod-aware unreachable including a clean putIfMatch failure, and the Mode.LOST arm), leaving M4.13 as the sweep that consumes it. Non-blocking: the ownership is at least recorded and traceable, which is the property that was missing.
